entries.title: Commanders' Terry McLaurin Gets Carted Off After a Leg Injury
entries.summary: The veteran wide receiver injured his left leg in the first quarter of Monday's game.
entries.content:
Commanders wide receiver Terry McLaurin was carted off the field after suffering a lower leg injury in the first quarter of Monday's game against the 49ers.

With Washington trailing 13-3, McLaurin appeared to get his feet tangled with San Francisco corner Deommodore Lenoir on a third-down route. McLaurin reached for his left leg as he fell to the ground. He stayed down for some time as trainers put an air cast on his left leg. Teammates looked on as he was carted off to the locker room. Shortly after, the Commanders ruled him out for the rest of Monday's game.

https://x.com/TSN_Sports/status/2112346540794601655?s=20
The veteran wideout was in his second game back after missing Week 4 with a hamstring injury. Entering Monday, he had 14 catches for 203 yards and a touchdown this season.

entries.title: Judge Rules That North Carolina’s Mail-In Ballot Restrictions Will Remain Through the Midterms
entries.summary: The state’s election board made it easier to reject completed ballots in an eleventh-hour change last month.
entries.content:
A federal judge ruled Wednesday that North Carolina’s rigid new mail-in ballot policies will remain in place for the midterms, upholding a last-minute rule change that could make it easier for state officials to invalidate thousands of votes in November.

U.S. District Judge Thomas Schroeder, a George W. Bush appointee, said that it was already too late to overturn the policies, which the state's Republican-led board of elections passed hours before voters received their ballots in early September.

“Neither of the two Challenged Provisions, which are clearly stated on the absentee ballot materials — that the voter sign his or her own name and place their ballot in a sealed envelope provided by the county board of election — is burdensome, much less unduly so,” Schroeder wrote.

The judge said in his ruling that the plaintiffs — a coalition of civil rights groups — waited too long to move for an injunction, filing the request the day before officials began counting absentee ballots.

“We’re in the midst of election season,” Schroeder said at a hearing last week.  

The decision upholds some of the strictest vote-by-mail procedures in the country on North Carolina voters, who were the first in the country this cycle to receive their ballots. Schroeder’s ruling also comes as national efforts to curb or question mail-in voting intensify before Nov. 3.

The new guidelines make it easier for the state to reject completed ballots over technicalities. The rules direct county officials to “spoil” mail-in ballots when the inner envelope is not sealed perfectly or when a voter’s signature does clearly match the name of an application number on the return envelope — even if the voter uses a nickname, maiden name or initials.

While election officials typically issue replacement ballots, the plaintiffs argued that voters whose errors are discovered close to Election Day rarely have enough time to submit a new one.

At a recent hearing, the plaintiff’s attorney Jacob Shelly said that most voters simply do not recast ballots after county officials declare them spoiled.

More than 123,000 voters had already submitted requests for absentee ballots as of Oct. 8, and 31,582 had been requested by the Oct. 14 hearing, according to court records. Absentee voting is largely utilized by overseas military service members and elderly and disabled voters. Shelly argued the new instructions lack clear standards and could produce inconsistent treatment across county lines.

“The Board’s new Republican majority rushed to implement eleventh-hour absentee ballot restrictions that will inevitably disenfranchise scores of North Carolina voters,” the plaintiffs argued. “They will invalidate thousands of qualified voters’ ballots in the November election unless enjoined,” the motion added.

Those rules will remain law at least through the midterms, per Schroeder’s Monday ruling.

In the order, the judge makes light of Shelly’s arguments to provide an alternative to the voting rules.

“Plaintiffs’ proposed remedy eliminates any verification of the signature, permitting a voter to sign anyone’s name to the certification, even ‘Mickey Mouse,’” he wrote.

North Carolina’s election board shifted to a 3–2 Republican majority in May 2025 after the state’s Republican auditor, Dave Boliek, gained appointment authority. The board approved the changes despite a state law putting them on hold a week prior, which Democratic Gov. Josh Stein called a “blatant circumvention of the law.”

The board’s messaging around the changes reflected talking points repeated by President Donald Trump, who has claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is unreliable and rife with voter fraud. The Supreme Court recently blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing new rules pushed by the president to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of the midterms.

North Carolina has rolled out increasingly rigid voting rules in recent years. The state passed voter ID laws in 2023, and requiring voters to fill out their ballots in the presence of two witnesses and attach a photo copy of their ID if they intend to vote by mail.

In-person early voting in the state kicked off last Thursday.

entries.title: The Commanders Can't Complete Their Comeback in a Loss to the 49ers
entries.summary: After a lifeless first half, Washington came within a score of undefeated San Francisco in a 23-17 defeat.
entries.content:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Despite being given several opportunities to pull off an improbable win against the undefeated 49ers, the Commanders came up short of a comeback in a 23-17 defeat on Monday Night Football.

Facing a third-and-long from San Francisco’s 40-yard line with six seconds left in the game, quarterback Jayden Daniels was sacked to provide an anticlimactic finish to a game that had plenty of twists and turns.

The Commanders trailed 23-3 midway through the third quarter, but were able to claw back within six points in the fourth. At one point, Washington appeared to take the lead on a long touchdown run from Jeremy McNichols, but it was called back by a penalty.

“I love their fight, but I'm sick about the ending,” coach Dan Quinn said. “When it's hard, I love their resolve. But to be the team that we need to be, we've got to be more consistent.”

Daniels finished 29 of 40 for 300 yards and two touchdowns. Touchdown catches by Stefon Diggs and Rachaad White gave Washington hope, but in the end it wasn’t enough. While the loss drops Washington to 1-4-1, Monday’s late surge marked a dramatic shift from a deflating first half.

The 49ers Christian McCaffrey (64 yards rushing and two touchdowns) and Mike Evans (94 yards receiving) took turns carving up Washington early, helping San Francisco get out to a 20-3 lead by halftime.

Washington’s offense didn’t reach the end zone until there were 15 seconds remaining in the third quarter. Its struggles were made worse by the loss of Pro Bowl receiver Terry McLaurin, who went down with a leg injury in the first quarter. The unit looked rudderless for much of the first half, generating just 90 yards and failing to convert on a third down before the break.

“We dug ourselves a hole,” Daniels said after the loss. “We’ve got to [put together] a full game, be a four-quarter team. You know, not just a half team.”

Washington started to show some signs of life in the third quarter. Daniels found Stefon Diggs for a one-yard touchdown pass and, after forcing a three-and-out on the next 49ers possession, Washington drove 80 yards down the field and scored again to pull within a six points.

But on the Commanders’ final drive, Daniels was pressured into an intentional grounding penalty with 16 seconds remaining, which cost his team a down and a crucial 10 seconds on the clock. Given one last shot at a Hail Mary, two 49er pass rushers combined for a sack as double zeros hit the scoreboard.

entries.title: String of Sexual Misconduct Scandals in the House Hasn’t Fast-tracked Ethics Reform
entries.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson canceled the pre-midterm House session, punting any action on changes to sexual misconduct rules.
entries.content:
Following a string of sexual misconduct scandals in the House earlier this year, lawmakers pledged to overhaul how the chamber — and Congress in general — handles allegations in order to protect staff.

But months have passed since the high-profile resignations of Reps. Eric Swalwell (D-California) and Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) following allegations of misconduct involving congressional aides — and Republican leadership has yet to prioritize any action on stricter ethics rules.

The day before House Speaker Mike Johnson canceled most of the House’s session in September, Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-New Mexico) and Kat Cammack (R-Florida) approached him in the chamber to let him know they wanted to introduce their long-awaited bipartisan ethics reform package before lawmakers left Washington before the election.

But Johnson was noncommittal.

“It hadn't been official that we weren't going to have the time to be able to finalize and do the last bit of work we needed, so I was still pushing for us getting something done,” Leger Fernández told The Washington Sun, recalling the Sept. 2 conversation. “He knew in his mind he was going to cancel. So he was saying, ‘Well, you know, we’ll get something done, but I don’t know.’”

The following morning, House Republican leadership sent out the official notice canceling two weeks of session, giving members more time to hit the campaign trail but cutting legislative business short.

Leger Fernández and Cammack, the chairs of the Democratic and Republican women’s caucuses, respectively, have been working on a legislative package to overhaul how the House addresses sexual misconduct allegations. The joint effort was announced by both Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in May, but it has repeatedly stalled due to the House schedule being cut short this fall.
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)“I repeatedly pointed out that I had thought we should get these done earlier, but the constant breaks and interruptions in the legislative session have meant we haven't been able to finalize the work,” Leger Fernández said.

Leger Fernández said that meant it was difficult to get input from staff: “We kept having to cancel steps that were important to move us forward.”

When House lawmakers return to Washington after the midterms, they will have just 20 legislative days in the Capitol to get anything done. That period is expected to be busy, particularly if Republicans lose the majority in one or both chambers of Congress: Lawmakers have to approve a spending bill since government funding runs out on Dec. 11, negotiate a must-pass Pentagon policy bill, and debate permitting reform and college sports legislation. Republicans are also weighing another reconciliation bill to pass their legislative agenda and extend the debt limit.

Cammack and Leger Fernández expect to introduce a package that would include proposals like prohibiting members from dating staffers (currently, they’re only barred from having romantic relationships with staff in their own offices), updating the Congressional Accountability Act (a law that requires Congress to follow employment laws that apply to the private sector), and creating a “one-stop shop” to make it easier for people to come forward with allegations, Cammack said. Both women’s caucuses have held multiple meetings and listening sessions with male and female staffers and members of Congress to come up with recommendations.

Given the crowded legislative calendar, even supporters pushing for action admit it’s likely to get punted.

“I’m not confident anything’s going to get done when we get back,” Rep. Nancy Mace (R-South Carolina) told The Sun. “It’s going to be a disaster. I mean, we’re going to be trying to get through as much as we can, hopefully, before the end of the year. I don’t know how much of an appetite there is for ethics reform.”

“I don’t think women are taken seriously on the hill. Period,” added Mace, who said she’d personally support the efforts.

A senior House Republican, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, concurred, telling The Sun that the lame-duck business “will more likely dictate” whether ethics reform gets brought to the floor.

Still, Cammack told The Sun that she and Leger Fernández are “committed to getting a product out the door on the floor and passed by the end of this year.”

Cammack recalled that Johnson told her and Leger Fernández “that this is a priority and that he is going to do everything he can to help us make sure that this gets wrapped up by the end of the year.” Johnson’s office did not comment for this story.
U.S. Congress (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)But Democratic lawmakers pointed to Johnson’s record on issues related to sexual misconduct as a reason why they believe ethics reform will not get done. They noted he refused to bring a bill to the floor to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein, and he took nearly five months after allegations against Gonzales first came out to call on him to not run for reelection. The speaker is also supporting Rep. Max Miller’s (R-Ohio) reelection campaign despite allegations of domestic violence made by his ex-wife, and he dismissed concerns related to Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida) after a judge issued a restraining order against him to protect his ex-girlfriend from “dating violence.”

“Anybody with ethics reform on their bingo card in the lame-duck session from Republicans should go get a new bingo card. It ain’t happening,” said one House Democrat, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “If it does, it would be a shock to the world, and inconsistent with the way the Republicans have led for the last two years.”

A second House Democrat said, “I hope [Cammack] is right. But I’m not holding my breath.”

Jeffries told reporters in late September that there is an “expectation that there is going to be decisive action that Congress takes in a bipartisan way on this issue as soon as we return.” While Johnson has not publicly made any commitments, he has been supportive of some of the measures floated by Cammack and Leger Fernández, such as barring members from having romantic or sexual relationships with congressional staffers.

Members of Congress have pushed for reforms in the next session starting in January. At a House Rules Committee hearing in September for members to make suggestions to the rules package for the upcoming Congress, some lawmakers pushed to ban members from dating any congressional staffer, to update members’ training to prevent sexual misconduct, and to amend members’ code of conduct to ensure there are clear consequences for sexual misconduct, including facing expulsion votes and getting removed from committees.

“We need due process,” Leger Fernández, a House Rules Committee member, said at the hearing.

Some of the provisions in the House package would need Senate action, which Cammack said could add difficulties.

“If I’m being honest, it appears that the Senate seems more intent on passing college sports reforms than actually doing the work that the House has sent them, so that’s pretty frustrating, which is why we’ve also talked about just a rules package that would be [a resolution] that would have impacted the House only, but we know that the issue of sexual misconduct is not exclusive to the House, it’s on Senate side too,” Cammack said.

Both Leger Fernández and Cammack said they haven’t formally introduced a bill because lawmakers haven’t been on Capitol Hill to discuss the details and generate support for it. They considered introducing one during one of the brief pro forma sessions, when one member presides and no significant business is conducted.

“This is about cleaning up the House,” Cammack said. “There’s so many things that people are unaware of. We recognized early on there would be an education campaign, so introducing in a pro forma doesn’t exactly help us in driving that awareness campaign.”

Outside groups pushing for ethics reforms have grown impatient with the delays.

“You’ve had several members who are no longer running for reelection because of the issue, and all of those members have either resigned or have decided not to seek reelection because of public pressure, not because of a process has demanded they leave, but because of the public saying we don’t want these people to come back,” said Emma Davidson Tribbs, founding director of the National Women’s Defense League. “The public wants the system to be adjusted, and, to me, that says that they should be taking this seriously.”
Congress Ethics Swalwell (3777x2518, AR: 1.50)Cheyenne Hunt, founder and executive director of Reckoning Action, told the Sun: “This is a story that women organizers know all too well: Our concerns and things that we take up as important are often put on the back burner.”

“I don’t have a profound amount of faith in Republicans prioritizing this in a lame-duck scenario,” she added.

Hunt, a lawyer and Democratic activist who played a key role in bringing allegations against Swalwell and former Maine Senate Democratic candidate Graham Platner to light, said that she anticipates that any sort of change would take place in the next Congress, where Democrats are expected to have control of at least one chamber. Leger Fernández told The Sun that House Democratic leadership has committed to scheduling a vote on ethics reform next year if they win the majority in November.

The fact that the process has not been prioritized by Republican leadership “sends a clear message to women that there is still very much an old boys club in Washington that is gumming up the gears here to try and make Capitol Hill a safer place to work,” Hunt added.

“That should make all of us uncomfortable,” Hunt continued.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 8
entries.summary: This week’s volleyball standouts include a steady libero, a do-it-all setter and a dominant outside hitter.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

This week’s set of standouts prove that anyone can make a difference on the volleyball court, no matter their position. Here are three locals who got the job done for their teams in a busy Week 8:

Mia Cheng, Senior, Libero, Clarksburg

Cheng, a three-year starter, is the engine driving the Coyotes through another strong regular season. Last week, her steady defensive play at libero helped Clarksburg beat Churchill and Poolesville, two of the best offensive teams in Montgomery County.

The wins helped coach Dawn Dickinson’s team clinch its division for the fourth year in a row. With just four games left in the regular season, Cheng and the Coyotes are well positioned to make a run out of the Maryland 4A West region. They also have a shot to make the county championship game in a few weeks.

“She totally takes control of the back row and the defense,” Dickinson said. “She’s just really stepped up and taken it upon herself to help the other players.”

Ayla Sayd, Senior, Outside Hitter, Marshall

Sayd produced an eye-popping stat line last week against Langley. In a back-and-forth, five-set slugfest on the road, Sayd tallied a season-high 33 kills in a victory. Her final two kills were the most important — with the Statesmen holding a slim 13-12 lead in the fifth set, Sayd’s 32nd and 33rd kills put the match away.

The victory avenged a 3-1 loss to the Saxons in late September. Sayd, an Elon commit, has finished with double-digit kills in every match she’s played this season and is up to 348 putaways on the year.

Jadyn Witt, Senior, Setter, Douglass

Before Douglass kicked off its volleyball campaign, Witt approached coach Tai Heath to request a position change. Her sophomore year, she played outside hitter for the Eagles. Last year, she transitioned to libero. This year, she wanted to try out the setter position.

“She’s very even-keeled, so I didn’t even question it,” Heath said. “If she wants to try setting she’s going to be perfectly fine. … I trust her.”

Heath’s trust in Witt has paid off for Douglass, which boasts an undefeated record. Her passing ability has helped the Eagles become one of the most dangerous offenses in Prince George’s County — Heath’s team has dropped just one set so far this season. In a recent bout against College Park Academy, Witt posted six assists, seven aces, five digs and three kills in a dominant three-set sweep.

entries.title: Polymarket Defended Its ‘Cornell Seven’ Trading Market — Then Took It Down
entries.summary: Congressional lawmakers criticized the prediction firm for initially permitting the bets.
entries.content:
The prediction market Polymarket has taken down a page allowing users to bet on the outcome of the “Cornell Seven” gang rape allegations, a reversal that followed public criticism from advocates for survivors’ rights.

On Sept. 30, Polymarket began allowing traders to predict whether the seven men accused in the Cornell University fraternity case would be criminally charged with a felony sex crime by January 2027. By Monday, traders had placed more than $450,000 in bets on the outcome, with more than 70% of users predicting there would not be charges.

In a statement to Front Office Sports, a publication focused on sports news, Polymarket initially defended the page, arguing that "markets bring better, unbiased information about important events, in contrast to the disinformation we’re all drowning in, which too often leaves the public misled and disillusioned to the point of apathy."

However, after Front Office Sports published a story and The Washington Sun requested comment, Polymarket reversed itself and removed the bet as an option.

Polymarket declined to comment when asked to explain why it reversed course.

The decision reflects the mounting scrutiny facing the prediction market industry. Polymarket has largely avoided regulatory scrutiny along with other online gambling companies, and it has hired the president's son Donald Trump Jr. as a strategic adviser as part of a broader Washington lobbying blitz.

However, congressional officials in both parties expressed concern about the “Cornell Seven” betting page in interviews with The Washington Sun.

“Prediction markets have existed for centuries, and there is an underlying logic to them. They proved more accurate in 2024 than the presidential polling,” said Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pennsylvania), a member of the House Ways and Means Committee. “However, like with any market, there also needs to be sensible regulation.”

Similarly, Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) said the option reflected that online gambling has gone too far.

“A proper country recognized the dangers of gambling,” Roy said. “Our nation today is embracing it and fails to realize they’re not watching the car wreck — they’re in it.”

Kalshi, Polymarket’s main competitor, said in a statement that it would not have allowed bets on the outcome of the case. It has banned gambling on missile strikes, kidnappings, deaths and rocket explosions.

It is unlikely that prediction markets will face much federal scrutiny anytime soon. The Federal Trade Commission recently began probing whether online sports gambling companies such as FanDuel and DraftKings promote deceptive or misleading advertisements. That probe is not expected to include the prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, which have been regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, led by a Trump appointee largely seen as supportive of industry.

Opponents of online gambling say the trading page on Cornell reflects the need for the companies to find ever more outlandish topics for bets to keep users entertained and on their platforms.

“You literally can gamble on anything right now, on the most perverse thing you can imagine,” said Les Bernal, the national director of Stop Predatory Gambling. “They’re constantly trying to keep people engaged constantly — every minute, every few seconds, so they continue to wager on these platforms.”

The Cornell trading page was also condemned by I Have the Right To, an advocacy group for survivors of sexual assault.
